messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur had spent forty years of his life believing in the fundamental order of things. As a prosecutor, he saw the law not just as a profession but as a bulwark against chaos, a system where actions had predictable consequences. That conviction shattered six months ago on a Tuesday evening. Walking home, he saw a group of teenagers vandalizing a bus stop and, drawing on a lifetime of authority, told them to stop. The situation escalated into a shouting match. When two police officers arrived, they saw an enraged older man and a group of youths. They heard only noise, a cacophony of overlapping accusations. Arthur tried to explain, to state his name and profession, but his words were lost in the incomprehensible chatter. The officers saw only a threat. One grabbed him, twisting his arm behind his back with a force that sent a shock of pain and humiliation through him. Pinned against his own car, listening to commands he couldn't distinguish from the general din, the bedrock of his world—that authority was rational and order would prevail—crumbled into dust.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel fundamentally unsafe. The courthouse, once his sanctuary of logic, became a landscape of potential threats. The low, overlapping hum of conversations in the cafeteria, once background noise, now registered as the same incomprehensible chatter from that night, immediately putting him on edge. The sight of a bailiff’s uniform or a passing police car would cause his heart to pound. When triggered by these reminders, his mind would flood with a sense of imminent danger. He became superalert, his gaze constantly sweeping across rooms, watching other people closely for any sign of aggression, any indication that the rules were about to break down again. He was certain that another unpredictable, violent encounter was just moments away, and he had to be the first to see it coming.

This pervasive sense of being on guard became exhausting, bleeding into every corner of his life. He found it nearly impossible to fall asleep, his mind replaying every perceived slight or potential danger from the day. To manage the feeling of threat that now shadowed him, Arthur developed a rigid set of routines. At the office, whenever the ambient noise felt too chaotic, he would retreat to his chambers and put on classical music so loud it drowned out everything else, a sensory shield against the world. At home, he began constantly scanning the street from his window and checking the locks on the doors. He started peppering his wife, Helen, with questions: "Did you hear that? Is everything alright?"—a constant need for reassurance that was beginning to wear on her patience. These weren't conscious decisions so much as desperate, automatic responses to a world he no longer trusted.

His strategies, meant to restore a sense of safety, instead began to feed the fear. The more he scanned his environment for signs of threat, the more he found. He would notice every minor instance of public misbehavior—a driver running a red light, someone cutting in line—and each one served as a fresh trigger, a reminder of the moral violation that started his ordeal. This constant checking made him hyper-aware of any police presence, spotting cruisers blocks away that he would have previously ignored. In turn, each trigger would amplify his feeling of being watchful and on guard, creating a vicious, self-sustaining loop. His attempts to control the threat were only making him more sensitive to it, ensuring he was never at peace. His world had shrunk to his home and his office, and even those places no longer felt secure.

The breaking point came last week. A junior attorney, trying to make small talk, told a lighthearted story involving a traffic stop. For Arthur, the mention of police, combined with the normal office chatter, was enough. He felt a surge of panic so intense he had to grip his desk to stay upright, convinced the room was closing in. The visible loss of composure in the place he commanded respect was a profound humiliation. He finally made an appointment because he felt he was losing the man he was—the confident, orderly prosecutor—to this new identity: a frightened, hypervigilant man who saw danger in every shadow. He told his wife he just wanted to feel normal again, to walk into a courtroom and not feel like a target.
